en: Record of the Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming during the Song Dynasty.
Zhili prostrates himself in humble reflection: In my youth, I yearned for learning and entered the path at Baoyun Monastery, where I encountered the transmission of the Dharma.
When my teacher lectured on this chapter, as my spiritual faculties were dull, I repeatedly consulted him regarding my doubts.
My former teacher, mindful of my diligent studies, did not refuse to guide me by holding my ear; thus, the meanings he explained I have roughly committed to memory.

Those of us who once heard the teachings together have now each grown old and infirm. Fearing that what we have previously seen may not benefit future generations, we have collectively striven—despite our lack of talent—to transcribe these works for the world.
However, as our understanding is dim and our knowledge limited, there may be errors in what has been transmitted; it is our hope that the sages of the Perfect School will edit and correct them.
This preface was completed on the first day of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Tianxi era, the year of Xinyou.
The *Mysterious Meaning of Guanyin* is presented here in brief; for the full version, it should be titled *The Mysterious Meaning of the Universal Gate Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara*.
Since both the preface and the main text fully clarify the persons and the teachings, I shall provide only a brief indication here.
As for the term "Profound Meaning" (*xuanyi*), it refers to the categories of meaning that are capable of explaining [the text].
"Xuan" (mysterious) is a term for that which is profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive.
"Yi" (meaning/principle) refers to that which possesses a deep underlying reason.

This was likely because the Great Master, through the power of samādhi, penetrated the ultimate limit of the dharma-nature and deeply perceived the intent regarding persons and dharmas within this chapter.
One should know that the five meanings, beginning with "name" (nāma), are all profound and subtle; the wisdom of those on the seven stages of expedient means (saptavidha-upāya) cannot perceive them.
Since this first volume consists of two fascicles, they are distinguished as "upper" and "lower."
Next, the person who was able to expound [this teaching] is shown: namely, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi.
Since this is a record of what he taught by his disciples, I did not dare to directly mention his formal dharma-name.
Mount Tiantai is the very place where the Great Master dwelt and entered into nirvana; thus, this location is used to manifest his person.

As for how the mountain acquired its name, the origins of his residence there, the circumstances of his passing, and the spiritual wonders that followed after his death, these are fully detailed in the *Daoben* (Great Biography), the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), the *Biezhuan* (Separate Biography), and other texts; they shall not be recounted here in full.

Regarding the name "Zhizhe" (Wisdom-Holder): after the Emperor of the Sui dynasty had completed his request to receive the Bodhisattva Mahāśīla, the Master said, "Your Majesty has diligently followed the holy prohibitions;
you should be titled 'Zongchi' (Dhāraṇī-Holder)."
The King said:
"The *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* states, 'One who transmits the lamp of the Buddha's Dharma is a wise one.
Since you, Master, have transmitted the lamp, you may be titled 'The Wise One' (Jñānabhadra)."
From this point forward, in all formal petitions and correspondence, he simply wrote, "The disciple Zongchi bows respectfully to the Wisdom-Knower (Zhizhe).
As for the title "Great Master" (Dashi), it was used because he was the teacher of emperors and high-ranking dignitaries; it was not the same as the titular ranks conferred in later times.

"Speaking" means to gladden; it refers to the unrestrained eloquence of joyful exposition and the delight in the realization of subtle awakening—this being quite different from other masters who merely cull from sūtras and śāstras to compose commentaries and sub-commentaries for the purpose of explicating the scriptural texts.
Therefore, when Dharma Master Darin saw the Venerable Zhiyi expounding the Dharma, he sighed to the assembly, saying:
"This is not something recorded in written commentaries; rather, it is the spontaneous eloquence resulting from his observation of the capacities of his audience."
Prajñā is neither dull nor sharp; sharpness or dullness arises from conditions. When it is abundant and timely, this constitutes its characteristic of sharpness;
when the pond is deep and the flowers are large, it is dull yet can be attained through the mind.

The record consists of the life and deeds of the Venerable Zhāng'ān, including his spiritual practices, miraculous manifestations, and activities from beginning to end, all of which are fully detailed in his original biography.
The commentary on the text is divided into two parts:
first, the commentary on the preface, which is further divided into two sections.
First, the description of how the True and Responsive Bodies benefit sentient beings, in two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of the True and Responsive Bodies, in two parts;
first, the demonstration of the wondrous functions of the two bodies, in three parts:
First, because the essence is wondrous, the two functions are extinguished; this has two parts.
First, the merging of phenomena leads to the extinction of responses.

Regarding "the perfect interfusion of the dharma-realm": because form and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, are identical to the nature itself, when one points to a single phenomenon, it universally encompasses all.

The universal inclusion of all phenomena is likewise so: each phenomenon permeates every other, such that there are no boundaries whatsoever; thus, it takes the absence of boundaries as its very boundary.

This Dharma-realm is entirely interfused—namely, the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, and the hundred suchnesses and thousand realms. Therefore, one may say "only matter, only mind," and "only the dependent, only the primary.
Were it otherwise, it would not be interfusion.

Avalokiteśvara realizes this as his fundamental essence; from this wondrous essence, he manifests responsive forms, responding to the capacities within the Dharma-realm by means of the Dharma-realm, and likewise evoking responses within the Dharma-realm through the capacities of the Dharma-realm.
In the Dharma-realm, subject and object are non-dual and naturally forgotten; if even the resonance and response are forgotten, how could essence and function be different?
Therefore, although a response is manifested, there is no response that can be maintained; thus it is said, "The image has nothing to be imaged."
2. From "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) onwards is the section on the true forgetting of the nature-purity.
Regarding "the purity of True Suchness," the *Awakening of Faith* states: "True Suchness refers to the mind-nature that is neither born nor extinguished."

Therefore, all dharmas from the very beginning have been free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; they are ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible. Being solely this one mind, it is called True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is further said: "This essence of true thusness (tathatā) has nothing that can be discarded, because all phenomena are entirely true;
nor is there anything that can be established, because all phenomena are identical with thusness."

Since it cannot be refuted or established, and one has personally severed speech and thought, it is fundamentally non-correspondent with the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; therefore, it is called "pure.

Avalokiteśvara takes this as his essential body and reveals this very body to all sentient beings, causing them to practice contemplation so that they may discern whether their vision is true or semblance-like; through such knowledge and vision, the benefit of subduing and severing [afflictions] is accomplished.

If one has not yet attained such knowledge and vision, yet is able to perfect the conditions for awakening through diligence in the three karmas and thereby transcend all suffering, they may also be called "transformed.
These are all manifestations of the True Body benefiting sentient beings.
Question:
That which shares the same object of perception is called "response" (yìng), while that which arises suddenly is termed "transformation" (huà).
These two types of bodies are both not the merit of wisdom; why, then, are they now described as being transformed into the true body?
Answer:
A transformation that occurs suddenly is a "transformation by manifestation" (*nirmāṇa-nirmāṇa*).
Here, in discussing transformations in relation to images, we take "transformation" to mean "transformative transformation" (*pariṇāma-nirmāṇa*).

Why is this so? It was stated above that regarding "images," both the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the response bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) are all images; from the self-realized reward body down to the bodies in the hells, all are already fully encompassed.

If one wishes to transform ordinary beings and sages and lead them into the state of holiness, it is necessary to manifest true wisdom; if it were not the true body, one could not effect such transformation.
Regarding the statement "transforming while there is nothing transformed," this is based on the equality of intrinsic nature, wherein one forgets the merit of transformation.
Although one causes those in the nine destinies to all proceed toward nirvana, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction.
The equal and true Dharma-realm: the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings; though he transforms beings all day long, all day long there is no transformation.
Second, from "Although like... onwards, it clarifies that because the function is forgotten, the two benefits are universally pervasive.
This has two parts: first, revealing the universality of the benefit.
Although all phenomena of form and mind lack an inherent nature of arising, they arise naturally through the harmony of causes and conditions.

Avalokiteśvara’s wondrous realization accords with the nature of all phenomena; though he possesses no physical form, when invoked by the various capacities of sentient beings, there is no manifestation that does not appear.
This is because, by severing all thoughts of deliberate response, one is able to respond universally to the myriad capacities within the Dharma-realm.
It is like a clear mirror that manifests images without thought; thus it is said that there is nothing that does not appear as its reflection.
2. From "Transformation is non-existent" (*huà wú*) downwards, the hidden benefit is universal.
The character "although" (*suī*) from above governs the beginning of this sentence.
Although the Middle Reality (*zhōngshí xìng*) cannot undergo transformation, it transforms while remaining unchanging; thus, delusion and enlightenment appear distinct.

Avalokiteśvara accords with principle; although he knows that [the nature of reality] is unchanging, he constantly employs true wisdom to transform all ordinary beings into non-dual sages. This is because he is devoid of any thought of "transforming beings"; thus, he universally causes others to overturn delusion and attain awakening, much like a magnet that attracts without intention. Therefore, it is said that there is nowhere he does not transform.

III. From "Therefore, there is no [location]" (*gu wu*) onwards, the section on "negating mutual illumination" (*zhe zhao xiang*) concludes the description of the virtues of the two bodies (*er shen de xiang*). This has two parts:
first, the characteristics of the *saṃbhogakāya* (*ying shen xiang*).
Because the Middle Way *dharmadhātu* simultaneously negates the two extremes, it has no location; because its very substance simultaneously illuminates both, it is not non-existent anywhere.

Regarding the phrase "the transformed body that responds to the nine destinies," here "transformed" (*hua*) is explained as appearing suddenly; together with "responding" (*ying*), these form two aspects, manifesting the sufficiency of its beneficial characteristics.
Question:
The Sūtra states, "If one is to be delivered by means of a Buddha-body, he manifests a Buddha-body.
Why, then, does it now speak of nine?
Answer:

The body of the Buddha-realm has both universal and restricted aspects. It is restricted to the body of the marks of the wisdom of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), for it exhaustively realizes the three thousandfold real marks.
This body is not even visible to the mental eye of those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*seng-que*); how much less so for those on lower stages or ordinary beings of the Small Vehicle?

Generally speaking, the marks at the stage of fruition in the three vehicles, as well as those seen by ordinary beings and sages in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), are all termed "Buddha-bodies" despite their distinctions of coarseness and subtlety.

However, because these are manifestations appearing according to the capacities of beings, they are what is perceived by the *savisaya-vijnana* (empirical consciousness) or the *karma-vijnana* (consciousness of karma); thus, although they are Buddha-bodies, they are generally categorized within the realms of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas.
The scriptural text follows the general sense, and thus speaks of "manifesting ten";
the present text follows the specific sense, and thus speaks of "nine paths.
Second, from the phrase "In the place of existence" onwards, the attainment of the True Body is explained.
Generally, the nine realms are designated as "existence" because they all possess karmic retribution.

Although the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) dwells within them, its true wisdom is inherently merged with the ultimate principle; therefore, it is said that it "tranquilizesly enters the meaning of non-duality."
The former is the true body manifesting responsive marks; this is the responsive marks revealing the true body.
Second, from "Therefore" onwards, it clarifies how these two functions encompass and sustain sentient beings.
Since the two functions of the True and the Responsive have been clarified above, I shall now demonstrate the manner in which they deliver beings from suffering and gather them into bliss.
The first two phrases clarify the True Body’s extraction of suffering; the subsequent two phrases indicate the Responsive Body’s bestowal of bliss.

In the Buddha’s response to the preceding question, it is shown that the three karmas manifest as a response from the unseen to the stimulus; through the seven calamities, the two requests, and the three poisons, one reaches the end of all suffering. Therefore, it is said: "One receives liberation from the precipice of suffering."

In answering the subsequent question, the Buddha’s three karmas manifest their response to accord with the hidden capacities [of beings]; thus, sentient beings in the three lands obtain tenfold benefits, ultimately returning to the secret treasury. Therefore, it is said: "To cause them to partake in the supreme bliss."
However, these four vows are not exclusively for the sake of bestowing happiness; although they are clarified here, they actually pertain to the preceding lines as well.

Since the three types of karma above are the causes that evoke [the response], and these four vows below clarify the basis for such responsiveness, the upper and lower sections mutually illuminate one another, with neither being deficient.
One should know that the three karmas also extend to latent capacities (*mingji*); although they may not manifest in the present, they must have been fully possessed in previous lives.
Second, from "Therefore, *sa*" onwards, there is a simultaneous clarification of the original and the manifested traces, in two parts:
first, showing the various names; second... [text continues].
First, regarding the title based on past and present causes:
the name "Fearless One" (Abhaya) used for this Sahā world appears twice in this sutra.
Amidst the perils of hostile bandits, one person cried out:
“Good sons! Do not be afraid.
You should all with one mind invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara; this Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings.”
It continues until it says, "By invoking his name, one immediately attains liberation.
Furthermore, within the exhortation to make offerings, the Buddha himself praises him, saying:
"This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness amidst terrors and urgent perils."
For this reason, all in this Sahā world call him the "Bestower of Fearlessness.

Regarding the phrase "Treasure Store" (*Ratnagarbha*) and so forth, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "In the past, during the Kalpa of Good Sustenance (*Sudhara*) in the world-system of Saṃtāraṇa, there was a Buddha named Ratnagarbha."
There was a wheel-turning king named Amitaviśuddha. His eldest crown prince made offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus for three months and resolved upon bodhicitta, vowing:

"If there be any sentient beings undergoing all manner of suffering, such as that of the three miserable realms, and they should be able to mindfully recollect me or invoke my name—such that I, through my divine ear and divine eye, hear and see them—and yet they are not relieved from their suffering, may I never attain unexcelled bodhi."
The Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"Because you observe all sentient beings and desire to sever their manifold sufferings, I now name you Avalokiteśvara.
II. From "Already Accomplished" onwards is the section on names from past and future lives.

Regarding the phrase "already accomplished" and so forth, the *Sahasrabhujasahasranetra Mahākaruṇā Sūtra* states: "The inconceivable power of the majestic spiritual authority of this Bodhisattva has already caused him to attain Buddhahood throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past; he was titled Tathāgata Saddharmaprabha. However, by the power of his great compassionate vows to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, he manifests as a Bodhisattva."
Furthermore, the *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi Sūtra* states: "He had already attained Buddhahood previously, being named the Tathāgata Saddharmaprabhāsa (Light of the True Dharma).
Śākyamuni served as that Buddha’s disciple while practicing asceticism."

Regarding the phrase "next he shall," the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states: "Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara shall next attain perfect enlightenment after Amitābha; his name shall be the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Merit Mountain King."
The term "Successor" (Buchu) carries the same meaning as that of a "Heir Apparent.
Second, from "Its Origin" onwards, the difficulty of fathoming [the Bodhisattva's nature] is concluded.

As stated in the aforementioned sutra, he is sometimes already a Tathāgata and sometimes manifests as a Bodhisattva; in past ages of the True Dharma, he once served as the teacher of Śākyamuni, and today Guanyin still fills the position of Amitābha.

Furthermore, just as Wondrous Virtue was originally the ninth-generation patriarch of the Benevolent One, while the descendant has already perfected the fruit and the patriarch still remains at the stage of cause, how can the relative heights and depths of their fundamental essence and manifested traces be measured?
However, one must employ the four phrases of high and low to manifest the inconceivable characteristics of the various sages.
Second, from "Now it is said" onwards, the section narrating the persons and the title of the teaching has two parts:
first, the narration of the persons including the word for "sūtra"; second... [text continues].
First, the introduction of the person, in two parts:
first, the transcription of the name from Sanskrit.

In various *dhāraṇī* sūtras, the Sanskrit name is first cited; the present text is somewhat abbreviated, yet its Chinese names frequently appear interchangeably: here he is called Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara), while elsewhere he is called Guanzizai (Avalokiteśvara).
Only the *Qianshouyan Dabeijing* refers to him as "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," and its meaning seems sufficient.
Nevertheless, when clarifying the resonance between the object and wisdom, these three characters [Guanshiyin] manifest the truth without deficiency.
If one follows the present interpretation, it has already manifested its own abiding.
Second, from "The Subject and Object" onwards, the meaning is explained by means of the Flower; this has two parts:
first, the individual explanations, which have two [subdivisions].
First, the explanation, in two parts:
first, the explanation of the character "contemplation" (guan), in two parts:
first, the subtle mastery of the Middle and the Extremes.
The perfect fusion of subject and object is the Middle Wisdom (*madhyama-jñāna*).
The simultaneous and thorough manifestation of both existence and non-existence is the Two Wisdoms (*dvaya-jñāna*).

Within a single mind, one simultaneously negates and illuminates; at the very moment of illumination, one penetrates the Two Truths, and thus it is said they are "simultaneously and thoroughly manifested."
Thus, the sounds and voices of the ten realms are simultaneously arising and observed, constantly obstructing and constantly illuminating.
Second, from "illuminating to the ultimate" below, both cultivation and nature are clarified.
To illuminate and exhaust the true nature is to see the virtue of the nature;
to examine its beginning and end is to see the virtue of cultivation.
This explains the sublime wisdom by means of the sublime object.

Although the inherent possession of the three thousand [dharmas] constitutes the three truths, they are combined here for the sake of practice and are thus referred to simply as the "True Nature" (*dharmatā*).

Within the context of cultivation, both the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the causes (*hetu*) each have their own fundamental and derivative aspects: joining the palms and bowing the head are the fundamental aspect of the conditions;
the adornment of merit and virtue is the derivative aspect of the conditions.
A single phrase or a single verse is the realization of the fundamental;
the adornment of wisdom is the realization of the derivative.
This is true for practice in accordance with the Way, and it is likewise true for practice in opposition to it.
When committing evil, how could the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the various mental factors not be its root?
When undergoing suffering, the fruit of habituation and the fruit of retribution are its branches.

If one discusses this root and branch in terms of the cultivated and the innate, the meaning reaches its ultimate limit: the "three thousand [dharmas] of innate virtue" exhausts the discussion of the root, while the "three thousand [dharmas] arising through cultivation" brings the discussion of the branches to their conclusion.

Without the three aforementioned types of wisdom, one cannot illuminate this realm; without this wondrous realm, one cannot give rise to that wisdom. They may be compared, for instance, to a box and its lid, or to water and milk.
Second, the explanation of "World-Sound" (Lokasvara).
This refers to the sounds of the ten realms of sentient beings encountering suffering and crying out for help by invoking the Name.

Regarding the phrase "the object of contemplation": while the aforementioned objects and wisdoms are both the subject of contemplation and can be compared to the hammer and anvil, this Sound of the World can be compared to the raw material itself.
If the wisdom of the preceding realm did not contemplate this World-Sound (Avalokiteśvara), how could it cause the ten realms to simultaneously be liberated from the three obstacles?
Furthermore, one should know that the wisdom of the preceding realm is precisely the inconceivable essence and function of the Bodhisattva; it is that which is capable of responding.
The realm of Avalokiteśvara is such that sentient beings, through their suffering, become the occasion for response; thus they are able to evoke it.
Within these three characters—realm, wisdom, and responsive resonance—all are fully accomplished.
"Ten thousand phenomena," and so forth, explains the world (*loka*).
"Various sounds and distinct songs" provides an explanation of sound (*śabda*) while retaining the reference to the world.
"All equally receive [the teaching] and leave suffering behind" refers to the attainment of benefit through the arousal of a spiritual response.
Second, from "Bodhisattva" onwards, the conclusion is evident.
Second, from "This is precisely" onwards, there is a general indication.
The three characters "contemplation" (*guan*) and so forth refer to the object and the wisdom (*jñāna*).
As for "subject" (*neng*) and "object" (*suo*), these refer to the response and the stimulus (*yinggan*).
"Subject" is that which responds, and "object" is that which is responded to; how could one redundantly speak of "that which illuminates" (*nengzhao*) and "that which is illuminated" (*suozhao*)?
2. Introduction to the Scripture.

Since this chapter has already circulated separately in the world, its title was originally often given as the *Guānshìyīn jīng* (Avalokiteśvara Sūtra) or the *Guānshìyīn Púsà Pǔmén pǐn jīng* (The Universal Gate Chapter of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Sūtra). Therefore, following the mention of the person's name, I shall now briefly explain the word "sūtra" (*jīng*).

Regarding the phrase "by way of meaning," the *Weimojing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) states: "Because they have passed through the minds and mouths of the sages, they are called 'sūtras' (*jing*).
As for the teachings that lead to the *siddhāntas*, because they have passed through the mind and mouth of the Tathāgata, they are named 'sūtras'."
It is further stated: "From the sages of antiquity to the sages of later times, there are none who have not attained the Way by means of the teachings expounded through these *siddhāntas*.
Regarding the phrase "principle and phrasing" (*wénlǐ*) and so forth, it adopts the sense of warp and woof, clarifying the Dharma through the interplay of analogy and illustration.
The warp and woof of the text mutually illuminate one another, weaving together the contemplative wisdom of the practitioner’s mind.
II. From "Universal Gate" (*Pumen*) onwards, the section narrating the dharma and including the chapter has two parts:
first, the narration of the dharma, which has two sub-parts: [End of provided text]
First, the two characters "eliminate" (xiao) are explained.
Second, from "employing one" (yong yi) onwards, the ten universals (shi pu) are shown.
As for "true reality" (shixiang): the three thousand [realms] are all real, and every aspect is perfectly interfused.

To speak of "one" is to signify non-duality. It is the collective designation for all virtues and an alternative name for the One Vehicle. The following ten meanings are presented to illustrate its characteristics: first, unconditional compassion; second, unconditioned great vows;

third, the practice of perfect cultivation; fourth, severance that is not severed; fifth, the perfectly integrated entry into the Dharma-gates; sixth, indeterminate supernatural powers; seventh, expedient means within the body of realization; eighth, the teaching of the Dharma through the opening of giving; ninth, universally making offerings to all Buddhas; and tenth, universally benefiting all sentient beings.
From the establishment of practice based on vows, this is the fruit arising from its own cause.
The entire essence gives rise to function, making offerings above and benefiting those below; from beginning to end, it encompasses all phenomena exhaustively.
All ten are the true mark (dharmatā), mutually penetrating and universally inclusive without obstruction.
2. Introduction to the Chapter.

Although this title was established according to its specific content, it is actually the "Circulation" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; therefore, I now introduce it so as not to forget its origin.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states: “*Varga*; this is translated as ‘chapter’ (*pin*), meaning that those items of similar meaning and category are collected into a single section.
Second, under the heading “Major Sections,” the main text is explained in two parts:
first, an illustration based on the major sections.
The explanations in the five chapters of the *Myōgen* (Miaoxuan) are extremely detailed; how could the wondrous meaning of this single chapter of the sutra differ?
That work merely clarifies that the five characters constitute a general title;

what we are now explaining is the specific title of this chapter. Furthermore, as they proceed in opposition [to our position], it is necessary to establish five distinct meanings for differentiation.
Although it establishes its own position, it must nevertheless correspond to that text which reveals the ultimate through the provisional—the perfect and wondrous teaching.

Thus, in explaining the name, it consists purely of the wondrous person and dharma; in revealing the essence, it is the non-dual principle and wisdom; in clarifying the core tenet, it is inconceivable response and resonance; in discussing its function, it is unconditioned bestowal and extraction; and in judging the hierarchy of teachings, it is the ultimate *amṛta* (clarified butter).
Regarding these five chapters, there are the general and specific names, and the general and specific classifications of the teachings, and so forth.
Second, from "Explanation of Names" (*shiming*) onwards, the present text is explained in five parts;
first, the explanation of names, which has four sections, the first of which is the listing of the chapters.
2. From "The 'pervasive' [person]" below, the characteristics are shown.
3. From "For what reason" below, it is matched to the faculties.
Since the pervasive type is brief, it is generally matched to those of sharp faculties;
If interpreted separately, the former is extensive, while the latter generally corresponds to those of dull faculties.
If one proceeds from the latter perspective, it is necessary to clarify the two types of retention (*dhāraṇī*).

For those who retain through hearing, extensive exposition is beneficial; for those who retain through meaning, concise exposition is beneficial. Those of dull faculties can grasp this through reflection.
Panthaka was called "dull" based on his hearing;
Maudgalyāyana was termed "dull" with respect to his realization of meaning.
Now, these two interpretations correspond to two different faculties; one must discuss their sharpness and dullness by alternating between the perspectives of hearing and meaning.
IV. From "Now, as for... onwards is the main explanation, in two parts:
first, the general explanation, in two parts;
first, the heading and enumeration, in two parts: [The text continues with the subsequent sections.]
First, the listing [of the four sections] below; second, the formal explanation, in four parts:
first, the listing of names, in three parts:
first, a brief indication.
2. The Intent of Establishing the Title, in two parts:
First, clarifying that the principle transcends names and numbers.

Although the Great Master employs ten categories of meaning to provide a general explanation of the title, he profoundly realizes that the Perfect Man Avalokiteśvara and the wondrous Dharma of the Universal Gate are fundamentally beyond the characteristics of verbal expression and mental conceptualization; hence he says, "The ultimate principle is pure," and so forth.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All verbal expressions are provisional names without reality; they merely follow deluded thoughts and cannot be apprehended.
Second, from "But it is wondrous" onwards, the numerical categories reveal the principle, which has two parts:
first, the demonstration by way of meaning.
The previous statement that the ultimate principle is pure, nameless, and devoid of characteristics was made in reference to self-realization, which transcends both speech and thought.

The present statement that the wondrous principle is empty and pervasive, explained through provisional names and characteristics, is discussed from the perspective of establishing teachings for the sake of sentient beings.

Regarding the term "void-pervasive" (*xū-tōng*): this clarifies that the wondrous principle has no fixed nature of abiding; although it lacks names and categories, it is able to universally respond to all names and categories.
Thus, Jingxi said:
"The nature is fundamentally nameless, yet it fully possesses all names; therefore, though there is nothing to be said, one speaks, and speaking thus constitutes the teaching."
Thus, both transcending words and relying on words accord with ultimate truth, for both the noble silence and the noble teaching are of great benefit.
The *Awakening of Faith* asks:
"If all dharmas are ineffable and inconceivable, how can sentient beings accord with them and thereby attain entry?"
Answer: If one knows that although all phenomena are spoken of, there is neither a speaker nor anything to be spoken;
and although they are contemplated, there is neither a contemplator nor anything to be contemplated—this is called "conformity."
"If one is free from discursive thought, it is called 'attaining entry.

First, the formal presentation:
regarding both contemplation (*guan*) and teaching (*jiao*), there are respective origins, and their sequence is not disordered.
Second, from "Regarding Contemplation" onwards, it clarifies the comprehensive inclusion.
Whether in contemplation or instruction, it is able to encompass and include all.
Contemplating the three minds in their totality: the mind of persons, dharmas, and compassion is the initial mind;
merit and wisdom are the middle mind.
The true [teachings] should extend to the eighth stage, all of which reside within the final mind.
When the conditions and causes reach their ultimate nature, the squareness and roundness of the causes are revealed; when wisdom and severance are fully perfected, the fruit is clearly complete.

Regarding the teachings, they are categorized into five periods, encompassing everything without exception: the *Avataṃsaka* represents the sudden teaching, while the three subsequent periods represent the gradual teaching.
Furthermore, within the gradual teaching, the Tripiṭaka belongs exclusively to the Small Vehicle, while the two *Sūtras* (the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saṃdhinirmocana*) belong to the Great Vehicle.
As for the *Lotus Sūtra*, it transcends the previous four flavors, because it is neither "exclusive" (*buta*) nor "combined" (*ken*), but rather "interwoven" (*taidai*).
Since all these explanations have already been provided, they are now abbreviated here.
Second, from "In terms of contemplation" (*yǎoguàn*) onwards, there is an explanation of two points, which is divided into two parts.
First, the sequence of contemplation (*guān cìdì*), which has ten sections:
First, regarding "Person and Dharma" (pudgala-dharma), there are two parts.
First, it serves as the heading for the nine pairs.
Since all nine topics, such as compassion and so forth, take person and dharma as their basis, these two are specifically highlighted in the title of this chapter.

Therefore, using the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) as an analogy for the provisional and the real: only when there is first a sentient being formed by the grasping of the aggregates (*skandha*) can one discuss their various virtues and conduct.
Since persons and dharmas encompass all nine categories [of existence], how could this principle not be so?
2. Regarding the section "Humanity and Dharmas" (*pudgala-dharma*) below, following the sequential order of the divisions, there are two parts;
first, the doubt:

"For what reason is 'humanity and dharmas' used as the sequence? [The answer is: Dharma is that which is mounted (*āruhya*), and humanity is that which mounts (*ārohaka*). Logically, it is appropriate to first explain the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) that is mounted, and only then discuss the initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) that is the mounter.
Now, why is this the reverse?
Second, from "This 'must'" onwards is the explanation:
there is no fixed order of priority between the one who mounts and that which is mounted.
Now there are two intentions for the sequence of the preceding masters' methods:
first, based on the scriptural text;
second, following the convenience of the meaning.
That a person can uphold the Dharma is precisely its meaning.
Second, compassion has two parts:
first, the sequence within the ten [perfections].
II. The Sequence of the Two Dharmas.
In all subsequent sections below, these two [points] serve as the standard pattern.

Next, regarding the discussion of compassion toward persons and dharmas: once the Great Being has contemplated the universal dharma of the fundamental nature and realized the principle that sentient beings and Buddhas are without difference, he observes that deluded beings undergo manifold sufferings in vain and have lost their original bliss; thus, he gives rise to vows to eternally bring about their deliverance and extraction from suffering.
Contemplating the objects of perception and generating the bodhicitta is precisely what follows next.
Regarding the sequence of compassion first and then pity, there are four explanations in the text.

Here, we follow the convenience of expression and the original intent, rather than the order of their functions or the practitioner's experience; therefore, the conclusion states: "Now, following the former meaning."

Third, regarding merit and wisdom, as for those who rely on faith in persons and dharmas: prior to aspiration and practice, one contemplates the perfected Dharma and achieves faith; based upon patient acceptance and joy, one establishes the Four Great Vows. If it were not for the mountain of practice, the ocean of vows could not be filled; thus, "practice" refers to the meaning of the Six Perfections, which comprise merit and wisdom.
The five [faculties] rely upon wisdom, and wisdom guides the five; they are like the eyes and feet, which cannot be lacking one for the other.
The five eliminate obstacles regarding phenomena, while wisdom dissolves delusions regarding principle; when the functions of these two are perfected, one realizes principle and attains phenomena.
Thus we know that merit and wisdom fulfill the preceding mind of compassion and give rise to the subsequent function of bestowing and extracting.
That merit comes first and wisdom follows is merely for the sake of linguistic convenience, not based on the original intent.
If we discuss the relationship between the conditions and the guide, what priority or sequence could there be?

Fourth, regarding the True and the Responsive: faith, aspiration, merit, and wisdom all reside within the cause; because the cause is capable of producing the fruit, they become the True and the Responsive.
Merit supports wisdom to manifest the True Body (dharmakāya), while wisdom guides merit to manifest the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya).

Regarding the sequence of the True and Responsive bodies: if one proceeds according to gradual transformation, one first displays the Responsive Body to accommodate those of lesser capacity, and only later leads them into the Reality before revealing the True Body.
It is also possible that the Real (the True) comes first and the Responsive (the Manifested) follows, such that the Real precedes and the Responsive succeeds.

However, we do not establish the sequence here based on the process of establishing transformations; rather, we establish the sequence by taking the manifestation of the Responsive from the Reality as our starting point. Therefore, it is said that [the Responsive] "follows" [the Real], which is also a matter of linguistic convenience.

5. Regarding the medicinal jewel: because the two practices of merit and wisdom manifest the True and the Responsive bodies, it is said that "it speaks directly of realization without yet involving those who benefit others.
Now, by clarifying the medicinal jewel, the characteristics of the two bodies benefiting sentient beings are demonstrated.
When the true body (dharmakāya) reveals its profound principle, the three delusions are all eliminated; this is the benefit of curing illness.
When the responsive body (nirmāṇakāya) accords with the perceptions of sentient beings, all manner of goodness gathers universally; this is the benefit of raining down jewels.

Regarding the statement "truly destroying the grasping of marks": since the three types of wisdom taking the principle as their object is what constitutes "the true," how could it merely destroy the grasping of marks related to *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* (view-delusions) and *bhāva-āsrava* (existence-delusions)?

One should know that *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* grasps the marks of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), the *paryavasthāna* of dust-like [delusions] grasps the mark of *nirvāṇa*, and ignorance (*avidyā*) grasps the marks of the two extremes; this applies to both the sequential and non-sequential [teachings].

Regarding the analogy that the medicinal herb and the jewel correspond respectively to compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*): the herb is equivalent to compassion, while the jewel may be categorized as loving-kindness. These two possess four meanings that establish their sequence: according to the fundamental intent of the teaching, loving-kindness comes first and compassion follows; yet from the perspective of practical application toward sentient beings, one first extracts [suffering] and subsequently bestows [happiness].
The current sequence resembles the latter two [of those three].

Sixth, regarding "the hidden and the manifest": the preceding explanation of the two bodies as dispelling delusions is like medicine, and their responding to capacities is like a jewel. Once the capacities have dispelled delusions, the true body becomes manifest; therefore, it is said that the two bodies are themselves what brings about the benefit of manifestation.

Now, it is explained that the two bodies are eternal and universally pervade all beings; those who see and know them are said to receive manifest benefit, while those who do not see or know them are said to receive hidden benefit.
Only by speaking in this way can one fully exhaust the characteristics of how the Sage benefits sentient beings.
The sequence of the two benefits cannot be definitively determined; they are also presented according to the convenience of expression, hence the terms "hidden" (*míng*) and "manifest" (*xiǎn*).
Since this is easily understood, it is not further discussed.

Seventh, regarding the provisional and the real, the fact that the prior conditions differ refers to the differences in the faculties and natures of the sentient beings who are the recipients of the teaching.
"Skillful means without fixed method" refers to the wisdom that discerns [reality], which has no fixed locus.

Whether acting in obscurity or in manifestation, whether destroying evil or generating good, these vary in depth and differ in breadth; yet all arise from the non-differentiated meeting of the two wisdoms. Therefore, regarding the benefit of future generations, one must discuss the provisional and the real.
Although there are three meanings regarding the sequence of the two types of wisdom, they are arranged here according to their relative depth.

Eighth, within the context of the fundamental and the trace, the phrase "skillfulness has degrees of superiority and inferiority" refers to the fact that wisdom possesses levels of loftiness and lowliness.
Regarding "superior, middling, and inferior": the state of *miao-jue* (wondrous enlightenment) is superior, *deng-jue* (equal enlightenment) is middling, and those below these are inferior.
Previously, when examining the capacities of beings through the provisional and the real, both must be employed simultaneously; hence it is called "horizontal" (*heng*).

Now, regarding the fundamental and the manifested (*ben-ji*) in terms of their stages, since high and low are discussed, a person must first follow the fundamental before manifesting the trace; hence it is called "vertical" (*shu*).
The sequence of these two dharmas can be observed.
Ninth, the condition as the cause (*ālambana-pratyaya*): two parts.
First, referring back to the preceding [section] to accord with the treatise regarding self and others.
The eight pairs mentioned above proceed from the subtle to the manifest; while they constitute a sequential discourse, they have not yet been systematically allocated.
Now, drawing back from the flow to seek the source, one must clarify the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) as the fundamental basis for the arising of all phenomena.

Second, to clarify the present investigation of the seeds: one traces back against the current to the person who possesses the wisdom, compassion, and vow-observance of the true body; fundamentally, they take the inherent quality (*prakṛti-guṇa*) as the cause for realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) to serve as the seed.
If the merit, compassion, and vows of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), which constitute the dharma of the universal gate, originally take the nature-virtues as their causal conditions and seeds,
then since this is the case for one's own practice, it serves as an analogy for transforming others.
The fundamental realization of true wisdom (pramāṇa-jñāna) silently benefits the King of Medicine, for its merit belongs to the seed of understanding;
the manifest transformation of expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna) clearly benefits the King of Jewels, for its efficacy is attributed to the seed of conditions.
Thus, the discussion proceeds from the perspective of the "conformity" (shun) to that of the "reversal" (que).
Tenth, regarding the discussion of wisdom and cessation (zhiduàn) through the sequence of conditions and fulfillment:
whereas previously we traced back in reverse until reaching the beginning of the causal virtues, we now proceed forward in order until reaching the culmination of the resultant virtues.
Thus, the sequence is established according to the beginning and the end; since there are no characters beyond "Tea" (茶), nothing further is discussed after the tenth.
Second, under the heading "The Two Summaries," the sequential order of the teaching is clarified in two parts:
first, citing the chapter to establish the framework.
2. Regarding "The General Meaning" (*tongyi*) below, there are two parts:
first, the general explanation.

Each of the five periods and four teachings can be discussed in terms of the ten [aspects], yet these are established according to their respective doctrines and meanings and cannot be exhaustively investigated.

Furthermore, regarding the ten pairs established by the Tripiṭaka: "person and dharma" refers to the person being formed by grasping the aggregates, and the dharma consisting of the truths and the means of crossing over; "compassion" refers to the conditioned objects for *śrāvakas* and the birth-conditions for *bodhisattvas*; "merit and wisdom" refers to the three trainings of the *śrāvaka* and the six perfections of the *bodhisattva*; "true and responsive" refers to the fivefold dharma-body acting through intentional manifestation; "medicine and jewel" refers to curing the diseases of the four abidings and raining down the jewels of the three vehicles; "hidden and manifest" refers to sentient beings gaining benefit whether they see and hear [the teaching] or do not see and hear it; "expedient and real" refers to the reality that accords with truth and the expedient that accords with worldly sentiment; "origin and trace" refers to self-realization as the origin and manifested appearance as the trace; and "condition and fulfillment" refers to a single phrase as the fulfilling cause and even a slight good deed as the conditioning seed; finally, "wisdom and severance" refers to the four fruits of the *śrāvaka* and the sudden attainment of the *bodhisattva*.
The Three Baskets (Tripitaka) are still preserved, and their general and specific characteristics can be known.
Second, regarding the section "Specific Now" and below, there are two parts:
first, the five flavors, which are further divided into two.
First, the explanation, in five parts:
first, milk, in two parts;
first, clarifying that it possesses the preceding six meanings.
Since "milk" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, it specifically indicates that sutra.
The distinct title of six characters fully incorporates both the Dharma and its metaphor:
"Mahāvaipulya" (Great Extensiveness) refers to the Dharma.
The Buddha is the person who has realized the fruit of Samantabhadra.
The *Avataṃsaka* is a metaphor for the causal flowers that adorn the meritorious virtues of the fruits of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Within this single title alone, six meanings are already contained.

From compassion up to the True and Responsive [Bodies], these do not transcend the causes and effects of one's own practice; the medicinal pearl, the hidden and the manifest, are merely the agent and object of transformation for others—this is a separate discussion of the six meanings within the Middle Way.
2. From "yet" (*er wei*) onwards, it clarifies the absence of the latter four meanings, in two parts:
first, clarifying the general and the specific, in two parts:
first, clarifying the absence of the specific.
Second, regarding the "General Meaning" below: it is permitted that there is a general application.

If one discusses the fundamental and the derivative, as well as the essence and function, by contrasting the Distinct and Perfect with the Provisional and Real, there is also a principle to be found in the scope of the subtle cause—the wisdom and severance of Great Enlightenment.
Second, from "For what reason" onwards, the deficiency [of the causal conditions] is clarified in two parts:
first, the deficiency is clarified at the beginning of the transformative teaching.

Regarding the four aspects—expedient means and reality, and so forth—the intention for appearing in the world is explained, the attainment of the distant past is revealed, and by tracing back the three causes, one ultimately returns to the Secret Treasury.

First, when the teachings were initially established, they were specifically intended to connect with those of great capacity; as this was not yet the ultimate consummation, that specific intention was omitted.
Second, from the words "The reason for this" (*so yi*) onwards, there is a detailed clarification of what is present and what is absent, in two parts:
first, a comparison with the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*).

Regarding the phrase "the small is separated from the great," the old translation of the *Saptatriṃśat-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "At that time, Śāriputra emerged from the Jeta Grove; he did not see the Tathāgata’s sovereign adornments and transformations, nor did he conceive such thoughts, nor did he delight in speaking of them or being able to praise them, because as a śrāvaka, he had already transcended the triple world."
This refers to the passage concerning being like one who is deaf or mute.
It is because, by not yet revealing the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he establishes provisional means (*upāya*), and by opening up those provisional means, he manifests the ultimate reality.
Regarding the phrase "having no origin or trace," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states at its beginning: "At the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he has just attained perfect awakening."

Now, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "All the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—think that Śākyamuni Buddha has now left the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, is sitting at the site of enlightenment and attaining perfect awakening."
"However, in truth, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
This is the passage from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that was suppressed.

Regarding the phrase "snapping fingers and clearing the throat": as described in the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers," Śākyamuni Buddha and the various emanated Buddhas extended their broad and long tongues up to the Brahma world, emitting immeasurable light from every pore that illuminated all worlds in the ten directions. After a full hundred thousand years, they withdrew their tongues and simultaneously cleared their throats and snapped their fingers together.
These two sounds reached throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, and the earth shook in six ways.
Then the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas who had emerged from the earth:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you should with a single mind receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, transcribe, and practice according to the teachings."

This refers to the fact that in this fundamental section, for the sake of entrusting the Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the earth, the Buddha manifests these supernatural powers to facilitate the transmission of the sutra.
The Commentary states that "clearing the throat" (kṣīṇ-kāśa) is a sign of thorough penetration and unobstructed flow.
"To snap one's fingers" signifies sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).

It expresses that the meaning of the Tathāgata’s distant origin has already been fully realized and communicated; it represents the Bodhisattva’s sympathetic joy upon hearing of this distant origin, whereby they increase their Path and diminish their births.
2. From "The absence of words" below, it is contrasted with the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "not clarifying the root-nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle," etc., this is because [this text] does not clarify—as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* does—that persons of the two vehicles and all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and shall all become Buddhas; therefore, it lacks the latter two pairs.
2. Next, regarding the section "Next, by way of" and below, concerning curdled milk (*dadhi*), there are two parts:
first, the Great Master’s explanation of the deficiency of the complete [set], which has two sub-sections;
first, the direct explanation of the deficiency of the complete set.
2. From "For what reason" onwards, the reason for the omission is clarified.

Regarding the term "teachings of the two vehicles," this is because the fruit of the *piṭaka* bodhisattvas is the same as that of the two vehicles; thus, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Āgamas* are generally referred to as "Śrāvaka sūtras."
This teaching does not discuss the reality of "wondrous existence" (miaoyou); therefore, when body and wisdom are extinguished, they cannot give rise to responsive manifestations.
Since there is neither true reality nor responsive manifestation, how could there be such things as medicinal herbs or magical pearls?
2. Regarding "My Own Difficulties" (*shinan*) below, there are two parts to Zhiyi’s (Zhang’an) personal analysis (*shiliaojian*):
first, the actual analysis, which has two parts;
first, the one who raises the difficulties.
Fearing that others might not understand the Great Master’s established distinction between the general and the particular, he has formulated this objection as a means to provide an exposition.
He thus raises the difficulty regarding the general and the particular in relation to the True and the Middle, because these two constitute the principle of the general and the particular.
Second, from "My Reply" onwards, the commentator explains:
[the term] "generally" (tong) does not refer to the Middle Way in contrast to the Ultimate Truth; rather, it refers generally to the Three Vehicles in contrast to the Bodhisattva specifically.
If one were to discuss the three baskets and three vehicles from cause to fruit, the ten meanings could be explained generally from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

However, in explaining Avalokiteśvara here, we must focus on the stage of the cause; in this teaching, the Bodhisattva at the causal stage possesses only the human qualities sought for Buddhahood—namely, the four vows of compassion, the six perfections of merit and wisdom, and the subduing of afflictions while they are not yet severed. Therefore, one cannot discuss the seven categories such as the True and Responsive bodies (*dharmakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth.
Not only are the seven [categories] of the Middle Way absent, but even the seven [categories] of the True Truth have not yet appeared.
Second, the section beginning with "The Master says" points to the Master’s intention.

In the *Zhiqi Sanzang Bie lun* (Treatise on the Distinct Stages of the Bodhisattva by Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Qi), the first three meanings differ from those of the two vehicles; they do not treat these three meanings separately in relation to the Middle Way.
Third is "fresh butter" (*navanīta*).

Although there are four teachings in terms of categories, here we contrast the partial and small with the great, the obscure and the manifest, the person and the dharma, and so forth—six pairs in total—and since the provisional traces have not yet been opened and the [hidden] meanings have not yet been investigated, there are no separate four [teachings].
4. Clarified Butter (*ghṛta*).
Although one may have realized the Small Dharma, one has not yet opened the minds of those of lesser capacity; this is similar to the previous two sections, which clarify only the six meanings.
5. From "If, according to... below, there is Ghee (*sarpir-manda*), in two parts:
First, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has two parts:
first, clarifying the eight meanings that distinguish this section.
Although six points are the same as before, there are not a few minor differences.

The former was the roundness that separated and biased, while this is the subtlety that opens up the coarse; thus, human relations, principles, teachings, and practices all converge in the One Vehicle, and the provisional and the real, as well as the original and the manifested, are revealed solely through this scripture.
If one discusses the provisional and the real in terms of self and other, or the partial and the complete, the former category is not without its place;

however, what is discussed here concerns the application of the provisional for the sake of the real, the opening of the provisional to reveal the real, the convergence of the provisional back to the real, and the abolition of the provisional to establish the real.
This combination of provisional and ultimate [teachings] is forever absent in other schools.

As for the fourfold aspects of principle and fact, principle and teaching, teaching and practice, and essence and function—regarding these fundamental and derivative stages, they may be found not only in this sutra but also in various other sections.

If the initial attainment of Buddhahood prior to *rajas-kalpa* eons ago is taken as the true origin, while all subsequent manifestations of attaining Buddhahood up to the present day are considered provisional traces, this is termed "the provisional and the real, the origin and the trace."
The opening of the Essential Gate (Honmon) being concluded, this very body is the fundamental (hon);
that which has already been taught in the Trace Gate (Jikimon), as well as all other sections, are called the trace (jaku).
This is what is meant by "the present fundamental and trace."
These two layers are beyond the scope of discussion in other sutras; therefore, it is said: "The various teachings do not clarify this, but the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone explains it.
Second, from "the three periods" onwards, it clarifies that the transformation [of beings] is complete for the duration of one kalpa.
Within the "Chapter on the Five Buddhas" in the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) chapter, each instance first provides expedient means and subsequently reveals the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Expedient means refers to the three teachings across the four periods, while the knowledge of all modes is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thus, it is known that the transformative work of all Buddhas culminates in this scripture.
Dīpaṃkara Kāśyapa appeared in a pure land, and thus he entered parinirvāṇa upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Now, the Buddha Śākyamuni appears in a defiled land; therefore, he preaches the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as a means of redeeming his life.
Second, "If we consider" [the following] regarding *nirvāṇa*, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that the gathering of sentient beings is exhaustive.
Those who have entered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* through gradual transformation are already dull compared to those previously mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who have not yet entered [the path] and must wait until they reach *nirvāṇa*; for them, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* remains beneficial.
However, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* breaks the great enemy ranks, while the *Nirvāṇa* gathers the remaining stragglers; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the harvest, whereas the *Nirvāṇa* is the gleaning.
The merit of the Great Transformation resided at Vulture Peak; because the capacities of others were not yet exhausted, he proceeded to the Twin Sala Trees.

Since those of the most dull faculties were still ignorant of the eight meanings of the *Lotus Sūtra*, it was necessary to clarify Buddha-nature in detail for such individuals; thus, the potential of this single era reached its ultimate conclusion here.
Second, from "If one discusses" onwards, it is clearly shown that there is no omission in the Dharma.

Since *Nirvāṇa* encompasses those of duller faculties, it begins by exhausting the fundamental nature and ends by manifesting the ultimate fruit; as the ten meanings are thus complete and sufficient, the three [aspects of] nature give rise to the three [aspects of] cultivation.

Since the cultivated nature consists of three aspects each, cause and effect are non-dual; that which is neither the conditional nor the perfect [wisdom] is precisely the essence of the Middle Way as the direct cause.
This direct essence must necessarily possess the virtue of dual illumination; therefore, upon the completion of cultivation, it becomes the Dharma-body of the three points (tri-bindu).

By extension, one should know that the conditions (pratyaya) and the fulfillment (pariniṣpatti) each also possess the three virtues of cultivation; it must be said that these are the three points of *prajñā* and the three points of *vimukti*, and so forth.

One should understand that in this present text, in order to accord with the two meanings of person and dharma in the title of the sutra, ten gates are established such that from beginning to end everything is twofold. This "two" is itself the non-dual within the midst [of duality]; thus, while the number may appear to increase or decrease, the Dharma itself neither increases nor decreases.
Therefore, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "The Śūraṅgama-samādhi exclusively cites one dharma that contains all dharmas without any deficiency; it is called the 'Secret Treasury.
Even in the case of the three dharmas of Nirvāṇa, which are fully complete, the dharmas are not many; this too is called the 'Secret Treasury.'"
This is because various sutras adapt to different conditions and capacities.
Second, regarding the section beginning with "This sequence," the conclusion states: "This sequence discusses the ten dharmas according to the five flavors. Question:

Previously, the ten dharmas were explained in terms of contemplation; from the initial stage of self-cultivation to the ultimate goal of transforming others, they truly constitute a sequential order in which their arising is not disordered.
Now, having traversed the five flavors, we have merely clarified the extent to which each section possesses the various dharmas; what, then, is the sequence of their successive arising?
Answer:

Previously, based on the perspective of contemplation (*guan*), we discussed the correct doctrine regarding the sequence of cultivation and realization. Now, based on the perspective of the teachings (*jiao*), we discuss their function and sequence, clarifying how these ten dharmas accord with the sequence of the sections and flavors to reach their respective capacities. From the first four flavors, which possess only three or six dharmas, up to the final *tāmapūra* (ghee), which possesses all eight or ten—how is this not a matter of function and sequence?

It should be understood that while the preceding section clarified the sequence of contemplative methods across various teachings, the present section clarifies the sequence of contemplative methods according to those teachings; although they differ in terms of their cultivation and application, both are entitled "the sequence of the ten dharmas."
Second, regarding the section "In terms of the four," as for the four teachings: in a general discussion, there are ten pairs for each of the *zhēn* (Truth) and *zhōng* (Middle) respectively.

If discussed specifically, the Tripiṭaka [teaching] applies separately to the Bodhisattva and possesses only three pairs: person and dharma, compassion and wisdom, and merit and wisdom. Because afflictions have not yet been severed, it lacks the meaning of the *zhēn* (True) and *yìng* (Response) and so forth, as fully explained previously.

By this example, the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*) may also be discussed separately in terms of the Bodhisattva regarding the six pairs of the True Truth (*satya*). From the seventh stage onward, as they vow to support residual habits, manifest births through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and transform sentient beings through the dual flow [of principle and phenomena], they attain the meanings of the true and the responsive, the medicinal pearl, and the hidden and the manifest.
The Two Vehicles do not possess this, and are therefore termed "distinct.

Although the practice of the Distinct Teaching proceeds in successive stages, one can clarify six meanings within it; generally, the characteristics of the three types of sages can be discerned therein.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, even the prior Perfect Teaching contains only six pairs; in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, all four teachings are known to contain ten pairs. Nevertheless, with respect to the "repeated application" (*punar-dāna*), there is no lack of progression.
The preceding discussion of the five flavors already contained the doctrinal meaning; therefore, it is said that "it can be understood.
Third, from "Therefore we know" onwards, there is the conclusion and praise of these two points, in two parts:
first, the conclusion and praise.
Regarding these ten [aspects], from the perspective of contemplation (*dhyāna*), there is the cause consisting of aspiration and practice, and the fruit consisting of power and capability.

Regarding these ten, from the perspective of teaching (*śāsana*), it is argued that the Dharma has a beginning and an end, and its application to sentient beings encompasses both the sharp and the dull faculties.
Therefore, for those who receive the teachings and cultivate contemplation, how could there be any who do not follow this path?
"To deliberate" (shānglüè) is synonymous with "to weigh and compare.
By means of these ten principles, one weighs and compares the teachings and contemplations of the entire lifetime of the Buddha's ministry; there is nothing that is not encompassed within them.
Because it represents the ultimate limit of cultivated virtue, it is said that "the spirit and resolve are vast and far-reaching.
Because it penetrates the foundation of the inherent qualities of nature, it is said that "its meaning and flavor are profound and deep."
Furthermore, it is called "vast and far-reaching" because it horizontally encompasses the four teachings;
it is called "profound and deep" because it vertically subsumes the five flavors.
It covers the ultimate reality of persons and dharmas, as well as the response [to beings], and the prior and posterior stages of one's own practice.
The medicinal beads range from the manifestation of the fundamental trace to the prior and subsequent [stages] of others;
they range from conditions and completion to wisdom and cessation, and from cultivation to nature, in terms of priority and sequence.
Three meanings are coarse, while six meanings are subtle; even eight meanings remain coarse, and ten meanings are most subtle.
This has been explained by distinguishing the coarse and the subtle through both brief and detailed treatment.
If one explains the coarse and the subtle by means of the "coarse" and the "sublime," the various flavors—whether pure or mixed—can be understood through reflection.
Second, from the section "Questioning the Dharma" onwards, there is a detailed analysis.

The intent of the question is this: prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vaipulya*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* were discussed separately; do they all equally possess the six meanings, or is there some difference in their intent?

Although the question concerns the similarities and differences among the three flavors and the six intentions, the answer details that within the flavor of curd there are three [stages] and within the flavor of clarified butter (ghṛta) there are eight. This is because among the five flavors, there are those with sharp and dull faculties; those with sharp faculties enter the flavor of clarified butter stage by stage, while those with dull faculties progress through the flavors in successive order.

Therefore, regarding the six meanings of the *Avataṃsaka*, those with the capacity of the "Mountain King" enter the stages and dwellings immediately; whereas the "poor son," being bewildered and distressed, still possesses the afflictions of view and thought in their entirety. Because the *Tripiṭaka* is merely Hinayāna, there are none therein who obtain the great benefit of the manifest [teaching].
If eighty thousand devas attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they are said to have "secretly departed.
As for those of the Two Vehicles, they are only now breaking through the afflictions of views and thoughts; thus, they merely produce curd.

Within the Vaipulya (Pafang) teachings, there are both praises and reproaches: those of sharp faculties who hear the praise immediately obtain the benefit of the Perfect [Vehicle], while those of lesser capacity who receive the reproach enter the gateway of the Shared [Vehicle] in secret.

In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the six intentions serve to refine and purify; those with keen faculties gain the unique benefit of realizing the perfect emptiness, while the Śrāvakas, through their transformative teaching, secretly shatter the sands of delusion.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the eight intentions harmonize those whose capacities have matured: the provisional gates are opened to reveal the ultimate truth, and the recent traces are discarded to allow them to see their original nature. Thus, those of dull faculties all attain the One Vehicle, while those of keen faculties further augment their holy path.
Because *nirvāṇa* is of a single flavor, it is not mentioned in detail; however, to gather and fully explain the ten pairs, even those of the most dull faculties obtain constant benefit.

Thus we know that although the four flavors discuss the varying depths of awakening according to the capacities of the practitioners, by the fifth period, the benefits received show no difference or gradation.
Without receiving the transmission from the Mountain Gate, how could one know the relationship between the various transformations of the Dharma and its teachings?
Third, the explanation has three parts:
first, a brief indication.
2. From "The person is" (*ren ji*) onwards is the extensive explanation, which has ten sections.
First, the person and the dharma, which has three parts.
First, establishing the object.
What is called "entry" refers to the sovereign within the aggregates (*skandha*).
Briefly discussed, there are four names: namely, self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), sentient being (*sattva*), and life-sustainer (*jīva*).

Fully discussed, there are sixteen, which are the aforementioned four plus twelve others: namely, the vital principle (*jīvaka*), the one who is born (*jantuka*), the nourisher (*poṣaka*), the multitude (*manuja*), the agent (*kāraka*), the one who causes to act (*kārayitṛ*), the originator (*utthāpaka*), the one who causes to originate (*utthāpayitṛ*), the experiencer (*vedaka*), the one who causes to experience (*vedayitṛ*), the knower (*jñātṛ*), and the seer (*paśyaka*).
As for what is called a "provisional name" (prajñapti), it has no substantial reality of its own, but is formed merely by relying on the combination of the five aggregates (skandhas).
It is like gathering the five fingers and provisionally naming them a "fist": thus, the fist exists by means of the fingers, yet the fingers do not constitute the fist.
The fist is like the person and the fingers are like the dharmas; that which is able to form [the fist] is real, while that which is formed is provisional.
This distinction between the provisional and the real is used to differentiate between permanence and impermanence according to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.

The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teaches that persons and dharmas ultimately revert to impermanence, whereas the Greater Vehicle (Mahāyāna) proclaims that both the provisional and the real are ultimately eternally abiding.
For instance, according to the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings, from the stage of ordinary beings up to the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, there exist both provisional persons and real dharmas;
however, upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, since both body and wisdom have been forgotten, where could a provisional person possibly reside?

In the Separate and Complete Teachings, when the three delusions and two deaths are completely purified, both person and dharma abide eternally and with sovereignty; the "person" is conventionally designated as the most honored of sentient beings, while the "real dharma" is termed the eternally abiding five aggregates.
To state it briefly: if one says that when delusions are exhausted, both person and phenomena are eternally non-existent, this is the Hīnayāna and is also termed the provisional teaching.
If one says that when delusions are exhausted, person and phenomena are not extinguished, this is the Mahāyāna and is also termed the ultimate teaching.

Generally speaking, when we speak of the Distinct and Perfect [teachings], those at the initial and final stages know the eternal; this is because they understand that persons and dharmas cannot be reduced to ashes or severed.
The Tripitaka and Shared [teachings] are the opposite, and are therefore said to be "ignorant.
Furthermore, one should know that the designations for "persons" are mostly established based on the real dharmas of the environment and its inhabitants.
As worldly people give appellations—whether based on physical appearance or on virtuous deeds—these are names established according to the actual dharmas of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
Or, whether based on place of residence or on administrative authority, these are names established according to the actual dharmas of the secondary environment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Now, if Avalokiteśvara is a provisional name, then "Avalokita" (Contemplation) is the wisdom of contemplation and "Śvara" (Sound) is the object; these constitute the primary retribution of oneself and others—how could they not be real dharmas?
However, because he is designated as the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara by name, he is classified as a person.
Since the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) is the vehicle upon which this person rides, it is classified as a phenomenon (dharma).
If one were to say "the Dharma Prince Samantamukha Avalokiteśvara," then one would instead have to classify the Universal Gate as a person and Avalokiteśvara as a phenomenon.

This is because this present chapter designates persons by means of the eye of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*); therefore, in explaining the meanings, all [terms] employ wisdom to designate persons.

One must understand that the essence of contemplative wisdom is a real dharma (*dravyadharma*). Since persons are designated by means of contemplative wisdom, then among the nine pairs—compassion, wisdom, truth, medicine, darkness, reality, the fundamental, awakening, and knowledge—all are real dharmas that designate their respective conventional persons (*prajñapti-pudgala*).
Now that this has been understood, all subsequent passages can be clearly seen.
Second, from "This... onwards is the explanation, which is divided into two parts:
first, a general indication, which is further divided into two.
First, it is shown that [the nature of reality] pervades both ordinary beings and sages.

Although there are differences in superiority and inferiority regarding the outflowing and non-outflowing, the partial and the perfect, and cause and effect, its provisional and real aspects are ultimately never lacking for even a moment.
2. From "If form... onwards, each section clarifies the provisional and the real, in two parts:
first, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

"Ordinary" (*fan*) refers to those who are common; "vulgar" (*bi*) refers to those who are base and evil. These are the individuals of the six destinies and five aggregates who constitute only the *pariccheda-janma* (segmented birth-and-death).
2. "Precepts and Concentration" and below concern the noble ones, which is twofold:
first, showing their characteristics.
Having already transformed from the ordinary to the noble, one immediately transmutes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) into the five factors of enlightenment (*pañca-bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Although the three vehicles and four teachings differ in their provisional and ultimate aspects, all are capable of transforming the *skandhas* into the *dharmakāya*, and according to their respective stages, they grasp the dharmas to constitute the conventional person.
Second, from "Therefore, Great" onwards, he cites scriptural evidence.

The stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), the ultimate point where the two attachments to self and phenomena are completely exhausted, is provisionally designated as "one thousand. All these attain the four virtues and are termed "unsurpassed sentient beings."
Based on the two thousand [dharmas] derived from the aggregates (*skandha*), each possesses four virtues and is termed the "unsurpassed true dharma.

Therefore, whether in the Hīnayāna, the Śrāvaka vehicle, or the Perfect [Teaching], there is nothing during the causal stage that is not the unsurpassed human dharma of the original nature; it is only because the two attachments have not been exhausted that their cultivation and attainment are not termed "unsurpassed."
2. From "Although it is common" onwards is the detailed explanation, which has two parts:
first, the ordinary person.
